questions.intro: AI features can make information more ACCESSIBLE: text-to-speech reads screens aloud, speech-to-text turns speech into captions or notes, tools can simplify complex text, describe images for people who are blind or have low vision, or translate. These can be life-changing. They also make mistakes: captions can mishear names or technical words, simplified text can drop important details, and image descriptions can be wrong or miss what matters. When the stakes are high, such as medical instructions or legal documents, check accessible versions against the original or with a trusted person.

sections.skill: Compare accessibility tools with a sign-language interpreter who is still learning

questions.prompt: What does the volunteer interpreter provide?

choices.text: Access to an event people could not follow otherwise
A perfect word-for-word record that never contains any mistakes or gaps

questions.correct_answer: Access to an event people could not follow otherwise
questions.intro: Imagine an event with a helpful volunteer interpreter who is still learning. Most of the time they convey the meaning well, which opens the event to people who could not follow it otherwise. But they sometimes miss a name or a technical term. For a casual talk that is fine; for a medical briefing, you would want a certified interpreter or a written copy to check. AI captions and descriptions are similar: valuable access, with occasional errors that matter more when stakes are high.

sections.skill: Recognize uneven accuracy and the need for accessible design

questions.prompt: A speech tool works well for one employee but poorly for a coworker with a strong accent. What does this show?

choices.text: Accents cannot be recognized at all
The coworker must be speaking incorrectly and should change the way they talk
The tool is perfect for everyone

questions.correct_answer: Accuracy can vary across speakers
questions.intro: Accessibility tools work better for some people and situations than others. Speech recognition may be less accurate for some accents, speech differences or noisy rooms; image descriptions may be vague for complex charts. People who rely on these tools should be able to correct errors and choose settings, and organizations should not treat automatic captions or descriptions as a complete substitute for accessible design, such as written alt text, real captions for important videos, and plain-language versions reviewed by people.
